1.sense: A man calls for the punishment he has been warned about, and the whole surah is the answer to that call. Saʾala with the preposition bi- reads as asking for a thing rather than asking about it, so the question is a dare. Wāqiʿ is an active participle from the verb for falling: what he asks for is not merely possible, it is already on its way down.

notes.t: The root s-ʾ-l runs through the surah and changes hands. Here a man asks for the punishment; at verse ten no intimate asks anything of another; at verse twenty-five the sāʾil is the poor man asking for food.
The Qur'an records the demand in its own words elsewhere, a challenge that Allah rain stones from the sky or bring on a painful punishment.
The exegetes name the questioner differently, an-Nadr ibn al-Harith most often, and some read the line as a statement about anyone who made the demand rather than about one man.
notes.src: at-Tabari records more than one name and does not settle between them

links.why: the same two words, wāqiʿ then dāfiʿ, in the same order across two verses
those who do not believe in the Hour are the ones who ask for it to be hurried

2.sense: The punishment is given an address before it is given a source. Dāfiʿ is the active participle of the verb for shoving a thing back, so what is denied is not escape but any agent at all who could hold it off. The demand of the first verse is granted in one sense, that the thing demanded is real, and refused in another, that there is any way out of it.

notes.t: The grammarians differ over what lil-kāfirīn attaches to. Read with wāqiʿ it means a punishment bound to fall upon the disbelievers; read with the verb of asking, the lām carries the sense of ʿan, and a questioner asked about the punishment.
The Qur'an answers the same impatience elsewhere: on the day it comes to them it is not turned aside, and the thing they mocked closes in around them.

links.why: a day with no turning back from Allah, no refuge and no denial

3.sense: The source is named, and the name gives the surah its title. Maʿārij is the plural of miʿrāj, the ladder or the flight of stairs, so the attribute is of the One who owns the ways up. Naming Him by the ascents sets up the next verse, which says who climbs them and how far it is.

notes.t: The only other place the word appears is of silver stairways in houses, an ordinary stair used as a picture of what worldly wealth amounts to. The ascents here belong to Allah rather than to anyone's roof.
Dhī is the construct of dhū, owner of, the form used across the Qur'an to attach an attribute to a name rather than a quality to a person: owner of the Throne, owner of the ways up.

links.why: raised in degrees, owner of the Throne, in a verse that also sends down the Spirit

4.sense: Taʿruju comes from the root of maʿārij, so the ascents just named are now being climbed. The angels and the Spirit go up to Him, and the climb is set against a day whose measure is fifty thousand years. The measure is given in human counting; it states the scale of the distance, not any delay on Allah's side.

notes.t: The same construction appears with a different figure, a day whose measure is a thousand years of what you count, describing the command going down and coming back up.
The angels and the Spirit are paired again in the Night of Decree, where the motion is the reverse: they come down with their Lord's permission.

The exegetes divide over both halves of the verse: whether ar-Rūḥ is Jibril or a creature distinct from the angels, and whether the fifty thousand years measures the length of the Day of Rising or the distance of the ascent itself.
notes.src: at-Tabari records both readings of ar-Rūḥ and both of the figure

links.why: a day with your Lord like a thousand years of what you count, in answer to men hurrying the punishment

5.sense: The address turns to the Prophet ﷺ, and the fa- ties the command to the distance just measured. The cognate accusative doubles the verb with its own noun, so the order is not simply to endure but to endure in a named manner. Jamīl is beauty of form, and patience that is jamīl is patience with no complaint carried to anyone but Allah.

notes.t: Yaʿqub uses the phrase twice when his sons come to him with the shirt and again years later, and the same account supplies the standing gloss of it: he complains of his anguish and grief to Allah alone.
The same adjective is attached to a different noun in a neighbouring surah, where the Prophet ﷺ is told to bear what they say and part from them with a beautiful parting.
The command is answered at the end of the surah by a second command about the same people, leave them to their wading and their play. Patience here and dismissal there frame everything between.

links.why: the other half of the instruction, given after the case against them is closed

6.sense: The pronoun goes back to the punishment that was demanded. They see it far away, far in time and so far as to be unreal. The verb is the verb of sight rather than of thought, which makes the distance a way of looking rather than an argument they have made.

notes.t: Baʿīd carries distance in space, distance in time and distance from possibility. Arabic uses it of a thing too remote to happen at all, and the exegetes read it here in that sense as much as in the temporal one.
The Qur'an states the opposite as fact: the reckoning has drawn near for mankind while they turn away heedless.

links.why: the guilty seeing the Fire and knowing they are falling into it, with no way turned aside

7.sense: The answer takes two words. The same verb of sight is used, so the two viewings are set side by side and the only difference is who is looking. What is far off in their eyes is near in the sight of the One who fixed the day.

notes.t: The two verses run on one pattern with every element swapped: their seeing against Ours, the pronoun far against the pronoun near. Nothing about the punishment changes between them.
The Prophet ﷺ is told to answer questions about the Hour by saying its knowledge is with Allah, and that for all he knows the Hour is near.

links.why: the Hour stated as having already drawn close

8.sense: The near thing now gets described, and the description begins at the top. Muhl is what settles at the bottom of a pot, the dregs of oil or the dross of molten metal, thick and hot and slow-moving. The sky, the one fixed ceiling overhead, is given the consistency of a liquid.

notes.t: The word appears three times in the Qur'an and the other two are drink: water like muhl that scalds the faces, and muhl boiling in the bellies. Here the same substance is overhead rather than in the mouth.
Yawma is in the accusative, hanging on the nearness of the previous verse. The scene is not a new sentence; it is the day that was just called near, opened out.

links.why: the same sky splitting and turning the colour of oiled leather

9.sense: ʿIhn is dyed wool teased apart into tufts. The mountains, the heaviest things a person can point at, are given the weight of something a breath would move. Sky and mountains are paired in these scenes because they are the two fixtures nobody expects to be told about.

notes.t: The phrase is repeated almost exactly in Al-Qariʿa, where the wool is specified as carded, teased loose with the fingers.

The Qur'an gives the mountains several ends: scattered as dust, set moving until they are a mirage, levelled to a plain with no dip or rise in it. The image here is of weight lost rather than of shape destroyed.

links.why: the same simile in the surah that pairs it with people scattered like moths

10.sense: The verb of the first verse comes back. There a man asked for the punishment; here nobody asks anybody anything. Ḥamīm is the intimate whose concern for you runs hot, and the word is set down twice so that both ends of the closest tie are named with one noun and neither end speaks.

notes.t: The root ḥ-m-m is heat. It gives the close friend, whose feeling for you is warm, and it gives the scalding water the people of the Fire are given to drink. The same form covers both.
The Qur'an says the wrongdoers have no ḥamīm and no intercessor who is heeded, and elsewhere that on that day there is no kinship between them and no asking after one another.

links.why: the regret in the Fire, no intercessors and no intimate friend

11.sense: They are made to see each other, so the silence of the previous verse is not from anyone being missing or unrecognised. The guilty man then begins a list of what he would hand over to buy his way out, and it opens with his children. Yaftadī is the verb for paying the ransom that frees a captive.

notes.t: The list runs outward in rings: sons, then wife and brother, then the branch of the clan that shelters him, then everyone on earth. Each step is further from him and each is offered as easily as the last.
The Qur'an closes the door on ransom in advance: no soul avails another, no intercession is accepted from it and no ransom is taken from it.

links.why: an earth's fill of gold offered as ransom and not accepted
the same relations named, and no father availing his child

12.sense: The ransom widens by one ring. Ṣāḥibah is literally the female companion, the one who keeps his company, and it is the Qur'an's ordinary word for a wife in scenes of this kind. Brother follows wife because the list is ordered by nearness of living rather than by blood.

notes.t: ʿAbasa runs the same relations in the opposite direction, a man fleeing his brother, his mother and father, his wife and his children. There he runs from them; here he would sell them.
Ṣāḥibah is built from ṣuḥbah, companionship, so the wife is named by the fact of being with him. It is the word being paid out, not the relationship.

links.why: the reason nobody is asked for anything: each man has a matter that occupies him

13.sense: Faṣīlah is the branch a man is cut off into within the tribe, the nearest circle past his own household. The relative clause names what that circle exists for: it takes him in. He offers to sell the shelter to escape what has come.

notes.t: The root f-ṣ-l is to separate a thing off. A faṣīlah is a segment cut from the larger body of the tribe, which is why the word means the near kin and not the whole people.
The verb of shelter, āwā, is used of what Allah did for the Prophet ﷺ, who was found an orphan and given shelter. The clan is not the source of that even where it looks like it.

links.why: the Prophet ﷺ ordered to warn this same nearest circle first

14.sense: The list ends by emptying the earth into the offer. Thumma holds the rescue apart from the payment, as though everyone alive were only the price and the saving a separate thing to be bought afterwards. The pronoun in yunjīh stays singular: all of that for one man.

notes.t: The Qur'an sets out the identical offer and refuses it, everything in the earth and its like again with it, given as ransom from the punishment of the Day of Rising, and not accepted.
The four verses of the ransom are a single sentence in Arabic, with bibanīhi and everything after it hanging on one verb. The grammar keeps him paying without ever reaching the point of being saved.

links.why: the same ransom offered by those who did not answer their Lord

15.sense: Kallā cuts the offer off before it can be made. Laẓā is a name of the Fire and also the bare flame itself, the tongue of fire with no smoke in it. The pronoun hā has nothing before it to refer to; the name arrives first and the thing is known by the name.

notes.t: Laẓā occurs only here in the Qur'an as a noun. The root shows up once more as a verb, in the warning of a fire that blazes, talaẓẓā.
Kallā appears twice in the surah, at this verse and at verse thirty-nine. Both times it refuses something the guilty are counting on: first the ransom, then a place in the Garden.

links.why: the same root as a verb, a fire that blazes, and the two men it sorts

16.sense: Nazzāʿah is the intensive of the verb for pulling a thing out by its root, and the form describes something that does this as its work rather than once. Shawā is the outer part of a body, the skin at the head and the ends of the limbs. The Fire is given the grammar of an agent with a single occupation.

notes.t: The exegetes gloss shawā three ways: the skin of the head, the extremities, and the outer covering of the body generally. All three are recorded and the word is rare enough that none of them can be checked against a second occurrence.
notes.src: at-Tabari carries the scalp, the limbs and the outer skin

notes.t: The intensive pattern faʿʿāl, here in its feminine, is the pattern of trades and habits in Arabic. It turns the tearing into what the Fire is for rather than what it happens to do.

17.sense: The Fire calls, and what it calls is described by two verbs of turning rather than by a name. Adbara is to present the back; tawallā is to turn from something you had been facing. The one who went away is the one summoned, and the summons goes out in the direction he took.

notes.t: Both verbs are used elsewhere of the same refusal: one man turned his back and grew proud, another turned away and gave a little then stopped.
A fire that calls is the surah's one figure of speech about the Fire itself. Everything else in the passage is what it does to a body; this is what it does to a person.

links.why: the same verb of turning the back, in the passage on the man who called the revelation sorcery

18.sense: Two more verbs, and the subject moves from posture to property. Jamaʿa is to collect; awʿā is to put a thing into a wiʿāʾ, a vessel, and shut it in. The fa- makes the second follow from the first, so the charge is not gathering on its own but sealing away what was gathered.

notes.t: A wiʿāʾ is a sack or container, the word used of the sacks searched in the story of Yusuf. Awʿā is to make a container of yourself.
The nearest parallel is the opening of Al-Humaza, the man who gathered wealth and counted it over and reckoned it would make him last.
The verse is answered inside the surah. At verse twenty-four the excepted are described by a known right in their wealth, which is the opposite of sealing.

links.why: the hoarding of gold and silver without spending it, and what the hoard becomes

19.sense: A general statement about the way the human being is put together. Halūʿ is an intensive form, and the surah does not leave it to the dictionary: the next two verses define it. The passive khuliqa places the trait at the making rather than at the choosing.

notes.t: Halūʿ occurs once in the Qur'an and is defined on the spot by the two verses after it. A word explained by its own text this way is rare.
Other verses state the same shape of thing about man: he was created of haste, and souls are brought face to face with their own tight-fistedness.

links.why: man praying for harm the way he prays for good, because he was made hasty

20.sense: The first half of the definition. Massa is the lightest verb of contact in Arabic, a touch rather than a blow, and what answers it is jazaʿ, the collapse of composure. The word is the standing opposite of the ṣabr the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to hold at verse five.

notes.t: Jazaʿ and ṣabr are set against each other directly in the Qur'an, in the words of the people of the Fire arguing among themselves: it is all one to us whether we panic or are patient, we have no escape.
The verse describes the same man as verse five in reverse. One is told to be patient with a beautiful patience; the other cannot take the touch of a hardship.

links.why: man never tiring of asking for good, then falling to despair when harm touches him

21.sense: The second half. The same verb of touching, the opposite thing touching him, and a reaction that is also a failure to bear what arrives: he closes his hand on it. Manūʿ is built on the same intensive pattern as halūʿ and jazūʿ, so all three name a settled disposition.

notes.t: Khayr in the Qur'an often means wealth in particular, as in the verse on bequests where a man leaves khayr behind, and in the description of man as fierce in his love of khayr.
The two verses give the definition a shape: harm arrives and he cannot hold himself together, good arrives and he will not let it go. Both are the same inability to bear what comes.

links.why: the same grasp described as an action rather than a disposition, gathering and sealing away

22.sense: The exception opens a list that runs to verse thirty-five. What is excepted from a trait built into the making is not a different kind of creature but a person held under a discipline. Prayer is named first, and the list will close on prayer again.

notes.t: The whole passage is the Qur'an's other list of the successful, the opening of Al-Muʾminun, with two clauses altered and one added. Reading them side by side shows what each surah does with the same material.
Al-ʿAsr runs the same sentence in miniature: man is at a loss, except those who, followed by a short list. The exception clause is the Qur'an's usual way of cutting a general verdict.

links.why: the same list opened from the other end, with success stated before the description

23.sense: Dāʾim is what continues without a break in it. The preposition ʿalā gives the sense of keeping to a thing and staying on it rather than merely doing it. The clause is the first of a run built on alladhīna hum, each one a fixed description rather than an occasional act.

notes.t: The Prophet ﷺ said that the deeds most beloved to Allah are the most constant of them, though they be few. The word he used, adwamuhā, is from the root of dāʾimūn here.
The exegetes read the constancy two ways: keeping the prayer at its times without letting it lapse, and stillness within the prayer itself. Both are recorded and the wording carries either.
notes.src: both glosses are carried in the classical tafsir

links.why: the other bracket of the list, the same prayer described as guarded rather than continuous

24.sense: The wealth is theirs and the claim on it is not. Ḥaqq is a due, a thing owed, and maʿlūm makes it fixed and measured rather than whatever generosity happens to allow. The clause answers verse eighteen directly: the man there gathered and sealed, and these keep a portion open.

notes.t: Adh-Dhariyat has almost the same sentence, a right in their wealth for the one who asks and the one deprived, and it comes there after a description of their nights in prayer, in the same order as here.

The exegetes differ over what the known right is. Some read it as zakah with its fixed rates; others hold it is a due beyond zakah, partly because the surah is Meccan and the obligation was legislated later.
Al-Muʾminun has an act at this point in the list, they are doers of zakah. Al-Maʿarij has a standing claim on property instead, which is the form the answer to verse eighteen has to take.

links.why: the same pairing of night prayer and a right in wealth, as a description of those who fear Allah

25.sense: Sāʾil returns from the first verse. There a man asked for the punishment; here a man asks for food, and the same word carries both. Maḥrūm is a passive participle, the one who has been cut off, and it is placed second so the due does not end with those who speak up.

notes.t: The surah's two askers stand at either end of the same word. The one in verse one asks for something to fall on him and is answered by the Fire; the one here asks for a share and is the reason the Garden is mentioned.

The glosses of maḥrūm differ: the poor man who does not beg and so is passed over, the man whose crop failed, the man left with no share in a distribution. The word says only that something was withheld from him.
notes.src: at-Tabari records several glosses without preferring one

links.why: the identical pair, in the surah's other statement of the same claim

26.sense: Ṣaddaqa is to hold a thing true and to say so, built from ṣidq, truthfulness. The object is the very day the questioner in verse one was demanding, so the list turns on the thing the opening mocked. Dīn here carries its sense of requital, the day accounts are settled.

notes.t: The Qur'an states the opposite with the matching verb, kadhdhaba, on the same object: you deny the Day of Judgment, and, have you seen the one who denies the Day of Judgment.
Yuṣaddiqūna is in the present tense while the clauses around it use participles. The affirming is an ongoing act, not a settled attribute like constancy or guarding.

links.why: what denying the Day looks like in conduct, driving away the orphan and not urging food for the poor

27.sense: Ishfāq is fear with care in it, the anxiety of someone who has a stake in how a thing turns out. Affirming the Day in the previous verse is followed at once by living underneath it. The punishment is attributed to their Lord, so the one feared is the one who raised and provided for them.

notes.t: The same participle describes those who are in dread of their Lord out of awe, in a passage that goes on to say they are the ones racing toward good.
The angels are described with the same word, in dread of Him, which places the emotion above the level of guilt. It is a response to who He is, not only to what one has done.

links.why: the believers in dread of the Hour set against those who ask for it to be hurried

28.sense: The reason for the dread, stated as a general truth rather than as a fact about them. Maʾmūn is the passive participle from amn, safety: nothing issues a guarantee against it. The line closes off the security that would turn the affirmation of verse twenty-six into a formality.

notes.t: The Qur'an puts the same point as a question and then as a verdict: do they feel safe from the plan of Allah, and none feels safe from the plan of Allah but the people who are lost.
This is the only clause in the list that is not a description of the excepted people. It steps out to explain the clause before it, then the list resumes.

links.why: the several directions the punishment can come from, none of them watched for

29.sense: Ḥāfiẓ is the guard set over a thing, the word used of keeping a trust or a deposit. Chastity is placed in the middle of the list, between the dread of the punishment and the keeping of pledges. The lām before furūjihim is the lām of purpose: they are guards for this, not merely guarders of it.

notes.t: The clause and the two verses after it are word for word the same as in Al-Muʾminun. Three consecutive verses are repeated in a second surah with nothing altered.
The same description is given to men and women in parallel in the list of those Allah has prepared forgiveness for, where the participle is used of both.

links.why: the same guarding stated as a command, with lowering the gaze attached to it

30.sense: The exception marks off the lawful place of what the previous verse guards. Mā malakat aymānuhum belongs to the legal order of the society the Qur'an first addressed, and its detail is worked out in the books of law rather than here. The verse states the matter in terms of blame: inside these bounds none attaches.

notes.t: The verse repeats 23:6 exactly, letter for letter. The pairing of the two passages is one of the clearest cases of a block of text placed in two surahs unchanged.
Ghayru malūmīn is a denial of blame rather than a grant of praise. The list returns to praise in the next clauses; this one only closes an exception.

31.sense: Warāʾa is what lies past a limit, the far side of a boundary line. ʿĀdūn comes from ʿadā, to step across, so the transgressor is named by the crossing rather than by the act itself. The sentence starts singular, whoever seeks, and finishes plural, those are the ones, which states the matter as a class rather than a case.

notes.t: The same root is used of the limits of Allah in the verse on divorce: those are the limits of Allah, do not cross them, and whoever crosses the limits of Allah, those are the wrongdoers. The grammar of that verse is the grammar of this one.
Ibtaghā is the eighth form of the root, seeking with effort. The verse is about the search past the boundary, not about stumbling over it.

links.why: the identical verse in its other setting

32.sense: Rāʿin is the herdsman, the one who watches a flock and answers for what happens to it. Amānah is what is handed to you to hold; ʿahd is what you gave your word to. Trusts stands in the plural against a pledge in the singular, which sets many deposits beside one covenant.

notes.t: The Prophet ﷺ said that every one of you is a rāʿin and every one of you is answerable for his flock, using the same word this verse uses. The image is of responsibility that comes with being placed over something.
notes.src: Bukhari and Muslim, from Ibn ʿUmar

notes.t: The Qur'an makes the delivering of trusts to their owners a command addressed to everyone, and joins it to judging between people with justice.

links.why: the identical clause in the parallel list

33.sense: Qāʾim is the one standing upright, and to stand with a testimony is to give it and not bend it. Shahādāt is plural, so each occasion of witness is counted on its own. Al-Muʾminun has this list without this clause, which makes testimony the addition Al-Maʿarij brings.

notes.t: The Qur'an joins the two words of this clause elsewhere in one command: be upholders of justice, witnesses for Allah, even against yourselves or your parents and kin.
The counterpart is stated as a prohibition, do not conceal the testimony, and whoever conceals it, his heart is sinful. Standing with a testimony is the opposite of sitting on it.
Placed between the pledge and the prayer, the clause sits where a duty owed to other people meets a duty owed to Allah. Testimony is the one act in the list that only exists in public.

links.why: the same standing, with the warning that hatred of a people must not push a witness off justice

34.sense: The list closes where it opened. Verse twenty-three had them constant in the prayer; here they guard it, and the third-form verb yuḥāfiẓūn describes a guarding kept up against whatever would wear it down. The same noun holds both ends of the list, with everything else set between them.

notes.t: The command form of this same verb is given in Al-Baqara, guard the prayers and the middle prayer, and stand before Allah in devotion.
Al-Muʾminun has the plural ṣalawāt in the matching clause where this surah has the singular ṣalāh, one of the few differences between the two lists.

links.why: the opening bracket, the prayer described as unbroken rather than defended

35.sense: The predicate the whole list has been waiting for since verse twenty-two. Mukram is a passive participle: the honour is done to them, not something they carry in. The word answers the humiliation that settles over faces in the last verse of the surah.

notes.t: The Qur'an uses mukramīn of the man from the far end of the city who was told to enter the Garden and wished his people knew what his Lord had done for him.

Al-Muʾminun closes its list with inheritance, they are the inheritors who will inherit Firdaws. Al-Maʿarij closes with honour, because the surah is about people who are being humiliated for what they say and hear.

links.why: the dhillah that covers the other faces, which this honour is set against

36.sense: The scene comes back to Mecca and to a gathering around the Prophet ﷺ. Muhṭiʿ is used of an animal running with its neck stretched out and its eyes fixed ahead. The question is not after information; it marks the gap between how eagerly they crowd in and how completely they refuse what they hear.

notes.t: The other two places the participle occurs are both on the Day of Rising: hurrying with heads raised and eyes not blinking, and hurrying toward the caller. The posture they take now is the posture they will be in then.
Mā and li are written joined as one word here, māli, one of only four places in the muṣḥaf where the interrogative is spelt that way.

links.why: the same question about the same people, answered with frightened donkeys fleeing a lion

37.sense: The crowd is described by where it sits and how it breaks up. ʿIzūn is the plural of ʿizah, a knot of people separated off from another knot. They come in clusters down both sides, which pictures a gathering that never becomes one body.

notes.t: ʿIzīn occurs once in the Qur'an. The singular ʿizah is a band of men attached to each other and detached from the rest, so the plural describes a crowd already broken into pieces before anything happens to it.
The nearest thing to it in form is ʿiḍīn, said of those who cut the Qur'an into parts. Both words describe a whole reduced to fragments.

38.sense: Ṭamaʿ is wanting something you think you have a claim on. The passive yudkhala is exact: nobody enters by his own doing, he is let in. The Garden was promised three verses earlier to people described by what they do, and these men expect the same end with none of it.

notes.t: Kullu imriʾin minhum breaks the clusters of the previous verse back into single men. The expectation is held one at a time even though the mockery is done in groups.
The Qur'an puts the same challenge to the believers themselves: did you suppose you would enter the Garden without what came to those before you.

links.why: the people the Garden was actually promised to, four verses earlier

39.sense: The second kallā of the surah refuses the expectation as the first refused the ransom. The answer given is their own origin: they are made from a substance they are perfectly aware of. Knowing where they came from is enough to settle what they can claim.

notes.t: The Qur'an makes the same argument at length elsewhere, telling man to look at what he was created from, and asking whether We did not create you from a despised fluid.
The verse leaves the substance unnamed and says only that they know it. The refusal works by withholding the word rather than by using it.

links.why: man seeing that he was made from a drop and turning into an open disputant

40.sense: An oath, sworn by the Lord of the points where the sun comes up and goes down. The plurals count a different rising place and setting place for every day of the year, so the oath is by the One who runs a moving order without a break in it. What the oath establishes is capability, and the next verse says what He is capable of.

notes.t: The Qur'an names this Lordship in the singular, the dual and the plural: Lord of the east and the west, Lord of the two easts and the two wests, and Lord of the risings here and in As-Saffat.
The grammarians read the lā in falā uqsimu two ways: an added particle that strengthens the oath, and a real negation that dismisses what the opponents have just been claiming before the oath begins.
notes.src: both readings are standard in the classical grammatical commentaries

links.why: the same plural risings, joined to the Lordship of the heavens and the earth

41.sense: The object of the ability: to put a better people in their place. Masbūq is the one overtaken in a race, the runner who comes in behind. Denying it says that nothing gets ahead of Allah, so the replacement is not a threat anyone can outrun by waiting or by planning.

notes.t: The other verse with bimasbūqīn runs the same two elements in the same order, We decreed death among you and We are not outrun, that We may replace you with your likes.

The Qur'an makes the replacement a standing possibility rather than a single threat: if you turn away He will substitute a people other than you, and if He wills He will take you away and bring others.

links.why: the same racing verb, do those who do evil suppose they will outstrip Us

42.sense: The command that completes the ṣabr of verse five: leave them to it. Khāḍa is to wade into water without knowing its depth, and the Qur'an uses it of plunging into idle talk about what one has not understood. Wading and play are set against the meeting, and the meeting is what ends the sentence.

notes.t: The verse appears word for word in Az-Zukhruf, closing that surah's argument in the same way this one closes.

The same instruction is given in a shorter form elsewhere, leave them in their wading, playing, and the people of the Fire name the habit among their own reasons for being there: we used to wade with those who waded.
Yakhūḍū and yalʿabū are jussive, hanging on the imperative before them. Grammatically their wading is the consequence of being let alone, which is the point of letting them alone.

links.why: the first half of the instruction, patience, given before the case was made

43.sense: The promised day is described by one motion: coming out fast. Ajdāth is the plural of jadath, a grave. The comparison is to men hurrying toward a nuṣb, a stone set upright as a mark, and the haste is the last echo of the crowd that came craning toward the Prophet ﷺ at verse thirty-six.

notes.t: The word nuṣub is read two ways: a stone set up and raced toward, the anṣāb the Qur'an names among the practices it forbids, and a banner or goal set up for a race. The verb yūfiḍūn occurs only here, which leaves the picture resting on the noun.
notes.src: at-Tabari carries the erected stone and the race-mark; the anṣāb are named at 5:90

notes.t: Al-Qamar has the same emergence with a different simile, coming out of the graves with lowered eyes like scattered locusts. That verse holds both halves of what this surah spreads over verses forty-three and forty-four.

links.why: the same graves, with the hurrying directed toward their Lord

44.sense: The eyes that were fixed on the Prophet ﷺ at verse thirty-six are down. Rahiqa is used of a thing that overtakes and then covers, so the humiliation settles over them like dust raised by their own running. The last sentence answers the first: the punishment a man asked to see has arrived, and it is named as the thing they were told about all along.

notes.t: The clause opens Al-Qalam's closing scene in the identical words, lowered their eyes, humiliation covering them, followed there by the reason: they used to be called to prostrate while they were sound.
The same verb and the same noun are used to describe what will not happen to the doers of good, no dust and no humiliation covering their faces.

The surah closes on the word it has been circling. Wāqiʿ in verse one made the punishment a thing already falling; yūʿadūn here makes it a thing already announced. Nothing between the two verses is new information.

links.why: the other faces on that day, dust on them and darkness covering it
